name: localtunnel
popularity: 22.5k GitHub stars, 1.6k forks, 408 npm dependents, decades-long name recognition as the original Node localtunnel port; still widely referenced in tutorials/StackOverflow.
maturity: Very popular historically but effectively in maintenance-only mode: recent commits are trivial README/link fixes, not feature or security work. npm package hasn't shipped a new version in ~5 years. The public hosted server (localtunnel.me) is known to be unreliable/overloaded (frequent community reports of downtime), and the project explicitly documents that a *separate* localtunnel/server repo powers the tunnel server, which is not actively developed either. Red flag: relying on the free public localtunnel.me service is not viable for a production feature; self-hosting the aging server code is possible but you inherit unmaintained infra code.
client_requirements: Client is simple and unprivileged: `npm install -g localtunnel` or `npx localtunnel --port N`, or `require('localtunnel')` programmatically. No admin/root or network interface changes needed; runs as an ordinary user-space Node process.
server_requirements: The npm 'localtunnel' package is CLIENT-only (a library you import to dial OUT to a tunnel server) - it does not export a server module. To use it for OUR use case (llama-server on user machine calling out, cloud SvelteKit backend receiving), the CLIENT side would run on the user's machine, but the SERVER side requires deploying and running the separate 'localtunnel/server' Node project as its own process/binary (its own HTTP+TCP listener, subdomain routing, port pool) - it cannot be mounted as a middleware inside an existing Express/SvelteKit adapter-node HTTP server. This means significant infra lift: a dedicated always-on server process, subdomain/DNS management, and monitoring, in addition to our own SvelteKit backend.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: The client library is easy and requires no admin rights, but the server-side is a separate unmaintained process we'd have to self-host and operate ourselves - it cannot be embedded in our existing SvelteKit/Node backend. Given our priority of minimal infra and no separate relay server, this adds real operational burden for a codebase that isn't being actively developed anymore.

name: Tunnelmole
license: Client: MIT. Hosted service/server: AGPLv3 (per README FAQ).
popularity: 1.9k GitHub stars, 124 forks, 17 npm dependents, actively promoted as an 'open source ngrok alternative'; has a marketing site (tunnelmole.com) and paid subscription tier for custom subdomains, suggesting a sustainable maintenance incentive.
maturity: Actively maintained relative to the older localtunnel forks - has CI, tests, telemetry/crash-reporting infra, a dashboard, and a companion self-hostable service repo (tunnelmole-service). Single-maintainer (Robbie Cahill) project, so bus-factor risk exists. Ships default telemetry (opt-out via env var) which is a minor privacy/ops consideration to disclose to end users.
client_requirements: Client install is simple and unprivileged for the JS path: `npm install --save tunnelmole` then `import { tunnelmole } from 'tunnelmole'; const url = await tunnelmole({port: N})`. Note the docs show `sudo npm install -g tunnelmole` for the CLI, but that's only needed for GLOBAL install convention (writing to system npm dir) - a local/project-scoped install or the precompiled binaries avoids sudo entirely. No network interface/root access required for tunnel operation itself.
server_requirements: Same architectural pattern as localtunnel: the 'tunnelmole' npm package installed via `npm install tunnelmole` exposes a CLIENT API (`import { tunnelmole } from 'tunnelmole'`) that runs on the machine being exposed (would run alongside llama-server locally) - it dials out to a hosted or self-hosted tunnel SERVER. The server component lives in a separate repo, 'tunnelmole-service', which must be run as its own process (their own hosted multi-tenant service, or self-hosted equivalent) - again NOT embeddable as a library inside our existing SvelteKit/Express HTTP server. Same infra burden pattern as localtunnel.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: More actively maintained than plain localtunnel, but architecturally identical: still a Node-only client + separately-run server, not embeddable in our SvelteKit backend process. Reliance on either a single-maintainer hosted service or self-hosting yet another relay server conflicts with our 'minimal infra, no separate binary' priority.

name: pipenet
license: See repo LICENSE file (README does not explicitly restate it in extracted text; repo shows a generic 'License' link, not confirmed MIT/other - flag as unverified pending direct file check).
popularity: 527 GitHub stars, 24 forks; used internally to power punkpeye's own 'mcp-proxy' project (a well-known MCP tool), lending some credibility; not yet as widely known as localtunnel/tunnelmole outside the MCP/AI tooling niche.
maturity: Newer and smaller community than localtunnel/tunnelmole (527 stars, single primary author 'punkpeye'/Frank Fiegel, sponsored by glama.ai), but explicitly positioned and marketed as an actively-maintained, modernized fork of localtunnel with TypeScript, ESM, and - critically - cloud-deployment-friendly single-port mode designed for exactly our scenario (running the tunnel server inside a container/PaaS with limited exposed ports). No long track record yet, so lower confidence in long-term maintenance, but design intent aligns very closely with our needs.
client_requirements: Fully unprivileged: `npm install pipenet` then `npx pipenet client --port 3000` or the programmatic client API. No admin/root, no network interface configuration, no daemon installation - pure JS library that 'just works' per the README's explicit zero-setup design goal (contrasted against zrok, which needs CLI-based environment init).
server_requirements: This is the key differentiator: pipenet ships BOTH client and server as importable JS/TS APIs in one npm package. Server side: `import { createServer } from 'pipenet/server'; const server = createServer({...}); server.listen(3000)` - this returns a Node http.Server-like object that can be embedded directly alongside (or wrapped by) our existing SvelteKit adapter-node server, or run as an internal service within our Node/Express backend, with lifecycle hooks (onTunnelCreated, onTunnelClosed, onRequest) that let us integrate auth/logging into our own request pipeline. It also explicitly supports 'single shared tunnel port' mode for containerized/cloud deployments (fly.io/Docker/K8s) which matches how our SvelteKit backend is likely deployed. Client side: `import { pipenet } from 'pipenet'; const tunnel = await pipenet({port: 3000, host: 'https://our-server.com'})` runs on the user's local machine to dial into our own server - no third-party hosted dependency needed at all since we run the server ourselves as part of our own infra.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Demoted from its prior top ranking for the same reason as h2tunnel: its core advantage was in-process embedding into our own Node server, which is no longer possible on serverless infrastructure — it now needs its own deployed service like any other tool here. Client requires Node.js, which is heavier than a static binary or OS-bundled SSH. Still a reasonable option given its purpose-built single-port cloud-deployment design, but no longer a standout.

name: progrium/localtunnel
language: Go (current v3 rewrite); earlier historical versions in Ruby+Python Twisted (v1) and Python gevent (v2)
popularity: 3.2k stars, 243 forks - notable mainly for historical/pioneering significance (it inspired ngrok and the entire localtunnel.me lineage), not for current active usage. Little to no real popularity signal as a currently-adopted tool.
maturity: Explicitly and openly declared unmaintained/legacy by its own author (progrium/Jeff Lindsay) in the README itself - the repo is kept mainly to archive project history, not for active use. v3 has 'no public server' set up and 'the scope of the project is pretty fixed where it is,' i.e., the author does not intend further development. This is the clearest maintenance red flag of all four options.
client_requirements: Would require installing/building a Go binary (`go install github.com/progrium/localtunnel`) on the end-user's machine - the client isn't distributed as prebuilt cross-platform binaries yet per the README ('Binary releases have not been set up yet'), so a typical non-technical end user would need Go tooling installed, which is a meaningfully higher and impractical bar than an npm-installable JS tool. Does not require admin/root or network interface changes, but the installation friction itself is a real usability problem for our target users.
server_requirements: Not applicable to a Node.js/SvelteKit integration at all in its current form: it is a Go program/library (via the author's Duplex framework), requires `go install` to build, and has no npm package, no JS bindings, and 'no public server' set up. Embedding it in our Node/SvelteKit backend would require either shelling out to a compiled Go binary as a separate process, or a full reimplementation in Node using the underlying protocol/design ideas - there is no library import path applicable to a JS project.
server_language: Go (current v3 rewrite); earlier historical versions in Ruby+Python Twisted (v1) and Python gevent (v2)
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Explicitly unmaintained by its own author, written in Go with no npm/JS bindings, no distributed public server, and no prebuilt cross-platform client binaries - it offers essentially zero direct integration value for a Node/SvelteKit stack beyond historical/architectural inspiration. Not viable as an off-the-shelf dependency; at best it's a design reference for our custom APLC-1 protocol.

name: wstunnel
language: Rust (v7+ rewrite; earlier versions in Haskell)
popularity: ~7.0k GitHub stars, 567 forks, 56 watchers - by far the most popular of the 4 tools surveyed. Has a dedicated docs site (wstunnel.erebe.eu), a public demo server, and commercial sponsorship. Widely referenced in firewall-bypass/DPI-evasion contexts and mentioned in various 'ngrok alternative' and censorship-circumvention roundups.
maturity: Actively maintained by a single core maintainer (erebe) with community PRs/forks (567). Project has a real history: started in Haskell, was fully rewritten to Rust in v7.0.0 for maintainability, which is itself a maturity signal (author cared enough to redo it rather than abandon it). Single-maintainer risk exists but project has been running for years with steady releases, static binaries, CI, docs, and sponsor (Service Planet) backing. No signs of abandonment.
client_requirements: Client is a single static binary (no interpreter/runtime needed), unprivileged - just run `wstunnel client ...` as a normal user process. Does not require admin/root and does not create virtual network interfaces (unlike VPN-style tools); it only opens local TCP listeners/forwards on ports the user is allowed to bind (high ports need no elevation). This is very close to ideal for our 'no admin' requirement, but it's still a foreign compiled binary the user must download/trust and keep updated, and we'd have to bundle/distribute per-OS/per-arch binaries ourselves.
server_requirements: Requires running a SEPARATE compiled Rust binary (wstunnel server) as its own OS process alongside the SvelteKit/Node app - it is NOT an embeddable Node/npm library, there is no way to run its server logic inside our existing Node HTTP process. On the cloud side we would need to: download/pin a wstunnel release binary (or build from source), run it as a systemd service or sidecar container, expose/manage its listening port, handle TLS certs (or rely on its auto-reload/self-signed cert feature), and route traffic between it and our Node app (e.g. wstunnel terminates the tunnel and forwards to a local TCP port that our Node app listens on, or vice versa). This is a genuine second service to deploy, monitor, restart on crash, and keep patched - it does not disappear into our existing process.
server_language: Rust (v7+ rewrite; earlier versions in Haskell)
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: The most mature and popular tool surveyed, with a single static Rust binary client requiring no admin/root and no runtime dependency (Node, Python, etc.) — as lean as a client gets short of reusing an OS-bundled tool like SSH. With the separate-server-process requirement now expected rather than disqualifying, this becomes a top recommendation; the one real caveat is its documented finickiness behind Nginx/Cloudflare/HAProxy, worth testing early against our actual serverless SvelteKit deployment's front door.

name: jprq
license: No LICENSE file found in repo (no explicit OSS license listed on GitHub 'Resources' - treat as unlicensed/all-rights-reserved by default)
popularity: ~1.5k stars, 213 forks, 15 watchers - moderate popularity, positioned explicitly as an 'ngrok-alternative/ngrok-replacement' (per GitHub topics), with install support via Homebrew, Scoop, and AUR, suggesting real historical adoption, but momentum appears to have stalled since the 2023 monetization pivot.
maturity: Red flags: the maintained hosted service (jprq.io) went members-only/paid in Oct 2023, meaning the free public service is effectively discontinued; project is single-maintainer (azimjohn) funded via 'buy me a coffee'; no license file makes self-hosting/forking legally ambiguous. It IS still described as 'open and free to self-host', so the code exists, but the primary maintained deployment path (hosted SaaS) is now gated, which is a strong abandonment/pivot signal for anyone wanting a drop-in dependency.
client_requirements: Client is a single compiled Go binary installed via package managers (brew/scoop/AUR) or manual download; runs unprivileged, no admin/root needed, no virtual network interface management - just a CLI that opens a local connection and calls `jprq http <port>` etc. Simple from the end-user's perspective, similar in spirit to wstunnel's client.
server_requirements: Requires running a SEPARATE compiled Go binary as a relay/tunnel server (the `server/` package with its own http_tunnel.go and tcp_tunnel.go), independent of and not embeddable in our Node process. We would need to build/deploy the Go server binary ourselves (self-host, since the public jprq.io is now gated), run it as its own service, handle subdomain routing and TLS/wildcard DNS ourselves, and monitor/restart it - functionally identical operational burden to wstunnel but with a smaller, less battle-tested, less-documented codebase and an ambiguous license.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Same 'separate relay binary' infra burden as wstunnel but with worse maturity signals: no clear license, apparent stalled development, and its hosted service pivoted to paid/members-only in 2023, meaning we'd be adopting an effectively unmaintained project and would own all future bugfixes ourselves. Not recommended.

name: cactus-tunnel
popularity: Only 58 stars/7 forks - the least popular of the four by a wide margin; published on npm as `cactus-tunnel` with an npm version badge and CI passing badge, listed in a couple of 'awesome-repositories' curation sites, but no major mentions found in broader ngrok-alternative roundups or notable adoption signals.
maturity: Small project (58 stars, 7 forks, 1 watcher) with a single primary maintainer (jeffreytse) but shows real recent feature development (bridge mode web UI, live dashboard, verbose logging, tests via Jest, CI badge for tests passing). Not abandoned, but very small community - classic single-maintainer risk: if jeffreytse stops maintaining it, there's little community depth to pick it up. No large-scale production adoption evidence found.
client_requirements: Client is `cactus-tunnel client <server> <target>`, distributed via npm, so the end-user machine needs Node.js >=22 installed (not a zero-dependency static binary like the Rust/Go tools) but runs as a normal unprivileged CLI process - no admin/root, no virtual network interfaces, no elevated capabilities. It also has a 'bridge mode' where the WebSocket relay can literally run inside a browser tab, which is a novel low-privilege option, though impractical for our headless llama-server use case. Requiring Node.js as a prerequisite is the main friction point versus wstunnel/jprq's zero-dependency static binaries - if our Python client wrapper doesn't already assume Node.js is present, this is an extra install step (still non-admin, but an added dependency).
server_requirements: This is the standout: it is a pure Node.js/TypeScript package (`npm install -g cactus-tunnel`, or `npm install cactus-tunnel` as a library) built on Express + websocket-stream + pump + winston. Its server mode (`cactusTunnel.Server`) is explicitly importable and instantiable as a JS/TS object (`new cactusTunnel.Server({ listen: {...} })`) - meaning the tunnel-server logic CAN run embedded inside our existing Node/SvelteKit HTTP process rather than as a separate OS binary/process. This directly satisfies our top infra priority: no separate relay binary to deploy/monitor/patch on its own - it's just another dependency in our existing package.json, sharing our Node runtime, our existing TLS termination, our existing deploy/monitoring/logging pipeline.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Demoted from its prior top ranking for the same architectural reason: the in-process-embedding advantage is moot on serverless infrastructure. Client requires Node.js >=22, heavier than a static binary. Smallest community of any option surveyed (58 stars), raising long-term maintenance risk relative to sish or wstunnel.

name: tunnelite
popularity: 92 stars, 8 forks, 5 watchers - modest but growing; distributed via NuGet (Tunnelite, Tunnelite.Sdk, Tunnelite.AspNetCore packages) with download-count badges, has its own hosted managed service at tunnelite.com (an 'open-source ngrok alternative'), and offers a first-class ASP.NET Core middleware (`app.UseTunnelite()`) - a notable adoption-friendliness signal for .NET shops, though not directly relevant to our Node/SvelteKit stack.
maturity: Actively developed right now (commits within days of this check), with real engineering depth: integration tests that spin up the tunnel server and a local app in-process to drive HTTP/SSE/WebSocket/TCP traffic, CI running on every PR, a CD pipeline deploying to Azure App Service, and a published homepage (tunnelite.com). Single-maintainer (cristipufu) project with modest star count, so still carries single-maintainer risk, but shows unusually strong test/CI discipline for its size and very recent commit velocity - lower abandonment risk than jprq or cactus-tunnel despite smaller star count.
client_requirements: Client is distributed as a NativeAOT-compiled CLI binary (or via NuGet as `Tunnelite` global tool / `dotnet tool install`), runs unprivileged with no admin/root or network-interface manipulation - conceptually as simple as the Rust/Go CLIs. There's also a `Tunnelite.Sdk` library for embedding tunnel-client logic directly into a .NET app and a `Tunnelite.AspNetCore` middleware for auto-tunneling ASP.NET apps - elegant if the local app were .NET, but our local component is Python/llama-server, so we'd just use the plain CLI binary or the SDK from a wrapped process, gaining no special advantage there.
server_requirements: Requires running a SEPARATE .NET server process (src/Tunnelite.Server) - it is a C#/.NET codebase built on SignalR/ASP.NET Core, which CANNOT run embedded inside our Node/SvelteKit process; there is no JS/TS interop path. Self-hosting requires: provisioning a .NET runtime (or NativeAOT binary) environment, wildcard SSL cert + wildcard DNS for subdomain routing (explicitly required per README), running/monitoring the ASP.NET Core server as its own service (their own reference deployment uses Azure App Service), and bridging it to our Node backend over HTTP/WebSocket at arm's length. This is the heaviest infra lift of the four for a Node-based team, since it also introduces an entirely different tech stack/runtime to operate (.NET) alongside our existing Node/Python stack.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Improved relative to its prior ranking: a separate server process is no longer a disqualifier, and its client is a lean NativeAOT-compiled single binary, comparable to wstunnel's static-binary approach. Still the heaviest server stack of the realistic options (a full .NET/SignalR/ASP.NET Core runtime distinct from anything else in our infrastructure, with a mandatory wildcard cert/DNS requirement and a reference deployment pinned to Azure App Service) — a real ops cost even though the client itself is lean.

name: sish
popularity: 4.7k GitHub stars, 335 forks, 54 watchers — clearly the most popular of the four tools surveyed, used in production by a public managed tunnel service.
maturity: Actively maintained, well-documented, production-oriented (used to run a managed public service tuns.sh, sponsored by pico.sh). No obvious red flags; healthy commit cadence, CI (golangci-lint), Docker images, binary releases.
client_requirements: Excellent — client-side needs literally nothing beyond a standard OpenSSH client already present on virtually every OS (`ssh -R 80:localhost:8080 tuns.sh`). No admin/root required, no special binary to install, no network interface management. This is the best-in-class client experience of all 4 options.
server_requirements: sish is a standalone Go SSH server binary (main.go, cmd/, sshmuxer/, httpmuxer/ packages) — it is NOT embeddable inside a Node.js process. It must run as a separate long-lived service/binary (or Docker container) on our cloud infra, listening on an SSH port (e.g. 2222) plus HTTP(S)/WS(S) ports for tunnel traffic, with its own TLS cert management, key-based auth files, and routing config. Our SvelteKit backend would sit behind/alongside it, or sish's HTTP muxer would need to front our app's routes — effectively adding a whole new infra component (process supervision, port allocation, key management, DNS wildcard) that must be deployed and operated independently from the Node app.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Best-in-class client of the entire survey (literally just OpenSSH, already present on every OS, zero install/admin) combined with a mature, actively-maintained, production-proven server (backs the public tuns.sh service). Now that a separate server binary/process is an accepted requirement rather than a penalty, sish's only real cost is standing up and operating one more Go service — no worse than any other option in this tier, and its client leanness is unmatched.

name: koding/tunnel
popularity: 331 stars, 69 forks — modest niche popularity from the ~2016 Koding platform era; not a widely adopted current standard.
maturity: Effectively abandoned/unmaintained. README itself states 'under active development, please vendor it if you want to use it' — a warning sign this was never considered stable, and now it has been stagnant for nearly a decade. No recent commits, no CI activity, low watcher count (18). Major red flag for adopting this as a foundational dependency in new infrastructure.
client_requirements: Client is also a Go binary/library (tunnel.NewClient) requiring a compiled Go client executable on the end-user's machine, or us cross-compiling and shipping a small Go binary for their OS/arch. No admin/root or interface management needed (pure userspace TCP dial), but it does require distributing and running a compiled binary rather than reusing something already installed — more client packaging burden than SSH-based sish.
server_requirements: This IS a Go library (not Node), so despite being conceptually a 'library not a binary,' it is NOT embeddable inside our Node.js/SvelteKit process at all — Go and Node are different runtimes with no in-process interop. To use koding/tunnel we would still need to write and run a separate Go binary/process on our cloud infra that imports tunnel.NewServer() and satisfies http.Handler, then either reverse-proxy Node traffic into it or run it as a sidecar in front of/behind the SvelteKit app. So in practice it has the same 'separate process required' infra lift as the other Go options — the 'library' framing only helps if your cloud backend is also Go, which ours is not.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Despite superficial appeal as a 'library,' koding/tunnel is a Go library usable only from Go processes — it cannot be embedded in our Node/SvelteKit server, so it doesn't reduce infra lift as hoped, and it also requires a separately built/shipped Go client binary. Combined with ~8 years of zero maintenance and an explicit 'vendor it, use at your own risk' warning in the README, this is not a viable choice.

name: h2tunnel
popularity: 142 stars, 4 forks — niche/early-stage project, much smaller community than sish or go-http-tunnel, but published on npm (h2tunnel) with real version history and active issue/PR engagement from the author.
maturity: Small but genuinely active project with a real author blog post explaining the design (boronine.com, June 2025), CI on GitHub Actions, test suite with coverage reporting, and recent dependency/security maintenance (dependabot bumps merged same year). Codebase is deliberately tiny ("less than 500 LOC", h2tunnel.ts) and zero-dependency, which minimizes supply-chain risk. Not battle-tested at scale (only 142 stars, 2 watchers) but the code is auditable in an afternoon given its size.
client_requirements: Also just an npm library — `import { TunnelClient } from "h2tunnel"` requires Node.js on the client machine. No admin/root or interface management needed — it's a pure userspace outbound TLS connection. Since the local wrapper is not required to stay Python, this is a non-issue: the client runs in the same runtime as the server, using the exact same library, protocol, and maintainer's test suite.
server_requirements: YES — this is the standout finding: h2tunnel exports a `TunnelServer` class directly usable as a plain Node.js library, no separate binary needed. Integration would be: `npm install h2tunnel`, then in our existing Node/adapter-node server process: `import { TunnelServer } from "h2tunnel"; const server = new TunnelServer({ key, cert, tunnelListenIp: "::0", tunnelListenPort: 15900, proxyListenIp: "::0", proxyListenPort: <port> }); server.start(); await server.waitUntilListening();` — roughly 10-20 lines of glue code to instantiate, start, and wire lifecycle (start on app boot, stop on shutdown), plus generating/rotating the mTLS cert+key pair (a few more lines using Node's crypto or a setup script). It listens on its OWN TCP ports (tunnelListenPort for client connections, proxyListenPort for public HTTP traffic) inside the SAME Node process — no separate deployable artifact, though it does need extra listening ports open on the same host/container as SvelteKit, and a reverse proxy (e.g. Caddy) or manual HTTP routing to stitch its proxied traffic into the SvelteKit app if we want a single public origin.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Demoted from its prior top ranking: its main advantage was embedding the server directly inside our own long-running Node process, which no longer exists now that the SvelteKit backend is serverless. It still must run as a separate deployed Node service like every other option, but its client requires a Node.js runtime rather than a lean static binary or an OS-bundled tool — heavier than sish or wstunnel on the client-leanness axis the user re-emphasized. Still worth considering for its small, auditable codebase and active maintenance.

name: go-http-tunnel
popularity: 3.3k stars, 312 forks, 61 watchers — the second most popular tool in this survey after sish, reflecting real historical adoption, though momentum has cooled.
maturity: Popular and historically well-regarded, but maintenance has clearly slowed to occasional dependency-bump commits rather than active feature development; author (mmatczuk, a recognized Go engineer) still merges occasional PRs. AGPL-3.0 license is a notable red flag/consideration: it requires that any network-service use of the code be made available in source form (with a paid "enterprise license" alternative offered by the author) — this has real legal/business implications for embedding it in a commercial SaaS backend.
client_requirements: Requires running the project's own compiled Go `tunnel` client binary on the end-user's machine (cross-compiled per OS/arch), authenticated via TLS client certificates. No root/admin or interface management needed — it's a normal userspace process — but like koding/tunnel, it means shipping/bundling an extra platform-specific binary alongside our Python client rather than reusing an existing installed tool.
server_requirements: Pure Go library/binary (cmd/ contains tunneld server and tunnel client binaries) — no Node interop possible. Would require deploying a separate Go binary (tunneld) as its own process/container on our cloud infrastructure, exposing its own TLS-terminated port for client connections and proxying HTTP/2-multiplexed traffic to our SvelteKit app's port, essentially the same 'extra service to build, deploy, and operate' pattern as go-http-tunnel's stablemates (sish, koding/tunnel). Additionally, the AGPL-3.0 license would legally obligate us to release our modifications/integration source (or purchase mmatczuk's enterprise license) since we'd be offering it as part of a network service — a meaningful business decision, not just an engineering one.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Technically solid HTTP/2-based multiplexing tunnel with decent adoption, but it fails the 'no separate infra' goal just as much as sish (a whole extra Go service to run and operate), it needs a bundled Go client binary rather than an already-installed tool, and critically its AGPL-3.0 license creates real legal exposure for a commercial SaaS backend unless we purchase an enterprise license. Not recommended given lower-friction alternatives exist.

name: localtunnel
popularity: localtunnel npm: 408 dependents, 33 versions (client pkg last published 5 years ago); server repo: 3.3k GitHub stars, 1.1k forks
maturity: Widely known (the original 'ngrok alternative'), but effectively unmaintained for years. Uses a bespoke HTTP-based tunnel protocol (client opens a raw TCP/HTTP connection to server, not literally a browser WebSocket) rather than the ws upgrade handshake. Server requires wildcard DNS (*.domain.tld) and listening on arbitrary OS-assigned TCP ports per client — architecturally heavier than embedding into an existing Express/SvelteKit HTTP listener.
client_requirements: There IS an existing Node.js client library (npm 'localtunnel'), but no official Python client. Go and C#/.NET community clients exist (gotunnelme, go-localtunnel, localtunnel-client for .NET) but no Python one was found. Would need to reverse-engineer/reimplement the wire protocol in Python.
server_requirements: High. localtunnel-server is not designed to run as embedded Express middleware — it's a standalone server.js process with its own port-per-client allocation logic and required wildcard subdomain DNS. Bolting this into an adapter-node SvelteKit app would mean running a second process alongside SvelteKit and reverse-proxying to it, not a clean 20-line integration. Realistically 200+ lines of adaptation work and infra changes (DNS, port ranges) if you tried to fold its logic in-process.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Conceptually the right pattern but wrong transport (raw TCP, not WS) and wrong deployment shape (standalone server needing wildcard DNS + dynamic port allocation, not embeddable middleware). Would require significant rework to embed in an existing SvelteKit/Node server and to write a Python client from scratch since the wire protocol isn't WebSocket-based.

name: tunnelmole
license: AGPL-3.0 (tunnelmole-service, per project docs) / client package license not explicitly restated on npm page
popularity: npm: 17 dependents, 92 versions; GitHub client repo stars in the low hundreds to low thousands range (exact count not captured from this page)
maturity: Open-source 'ngrok alternative', actively marketed, has a hosted service plus a self-hostable server (tunnelmole-service). More recently maintained than localtunnel. Also importable/embeddable as a Node dependency to programmatically start a tunnel client (not server) inside your own app.
client_requirements: Existing npm/Node client only; no Python client. The end-user's local machine would need Node.js and this npm package, OR we'd need to write a Python client implementing the same wire protocol as tunnelmole-service (protocol details not verified in this pass).
server_requirements: The client side is trivial to embed (a few lines: `import {tunnelmole} from 'tunnelmole'; await tunnelmole({port})`), but that's the wrong side for our use case (we need the SERVER logic embedded in the SvelteKit backend, not the client). The tunnelmole-service (server) was not confirmed to be embeddable middleware; treat as a standalone service similar to localtunnel-server — likely comparable integration cost (100+ lines / separate process).
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Good UX and more recently maintained than localtunnel, but the reusable/embeddable piece here is the CLIENT (Node-only), which is the wrong side for us since our need is a Python client talking to an embedded server library. The actual tunnel SERVER (tunnelmole-service) wasn't confirmed as embeddable middleware.

name: http-proxy
popularity: 3,347 dependents on npm (very widely used); underlying GitHub repo has tens of thousands of stars (http-party/node-http-proxy)
maturity: Extremely mature and battle-tested generic HTTP/WS proxy library, embeddable via `proxy.web(req,res,{target})` and `proxy.ws(req,socket,head,{target})`.
client_requirements: None — it's server-only and assumes the target is directly reachable, which is exactly the constraint we don't have (client is behind NAT/firewall).
server_requirements: N/A for our use case — would only be relevant as a building block if paired with custom multiplexing logic on top, not as a drop-in tunnel solution. As a plain reverse proxy it's ~10-20 lines to wire into Express, but that's not what we need.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Included because it repeatedly surfaces in 'websocket reverse proxy npm' searches, but it is explicitly the generic-proxy case the task warned about — not a NAT-traversal reverse-tunnel tool. Not viable for APLC-1 replacement, though its `ws()` proxying code could inform how to plumb WS upgrades if we build our own.

name: primus
popularity: 137 dependents on npm, 109 published versions
maturity: Mature, long-lived abstraction layer over multiple realtime transports (ws, engine.io, SockJS, uws, etc.) with built-in reconnect/heartbeat protocol (`primus::ping`/`primus::pong`). Has real protocol documentation making a from-scratch client feasible.
client_requirements: No Python client exists; Primus's client is JS-only (browser or Node). Its documented text protocol (`primus::ping::<epoch>`, `primus::pong::<epoch>`, etc.) is simple enough that a Python client COULD be hand-written against it if we chose to build our own tunnel logic using Primus purely as the reconnecting-transport layer.
server_requirements: Trivial to attach to an existing http.Server (`new Primus(server, options)`), roughly 5-10 lines, but doesn't solve the tunneling/multiplexing problem — would only be useful as the transport layer if we build APLC-1 ourselves on top of it (handles reconnect/heartbeat framing for us).
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Useful as a reconnect/heartbeat transport primitive to borrow from, not as a ready-made reverse-tunnel solution. Would still require us to build the entire request-multiplexing/routing logic (i.e., most of APLC-1) on top of it ourselves.

name: yamux
popularity: 0 dependents, 2 published versions
maturity: Essentially abandoned toy/proof-of-concept implementation of a stream multiplexer, requires Node v0.10.x (ancient). Not usable in a modern project.
client_requirements: N/A — package is effectively dead. Note also that this npm package has no relation to HashiCorp's actual Yamux multiplexing protocol used in libp2p/consul despite sharing the name; there is no official 'yamux' npm implementation of that real protocol either.
server_requirements: Not usable as-is (incompatible with modern Node); would need to find a modern replacement (e.g. reimplement HashiCorp's real 'yamux' protocol, which this npm package is NOT actually related to despite the name) or use another multiplexing lib.
has_programmable_api: see server_requirements notes
viability_notes: Dead package, wrong/misleading name-match to the real Yamux protocol, requires Node 0.10. Not usable. Confirms there is no mature, modern npm library implementing true stream multiplexing-over-WebSocket ready to embed.

name: Telebit
popularity: Very low on its own git host: 2 stars, 1 fork, 1 watcher on git.coolaj86.com (a self-hosted Gitea, not GitHub, so visibility/discoverability is minimal). No GitHub mirror with meaningful star count found. Single-maintainer project (AJ ONeal / coolaj86) promoted mainly via his own blog/talks.
maturity: Surprisingly still receiving commits: latest commit 2025-10-26 (version bump to v0.20.251025), 523 commits total on the 'stable' branch, 72 tags. However most feature work (README, lib, client code) dates to 2018-2019; recent commits look like small maintenance/packaging bumps rather than active feature development. Hosted service (telebit.cloud) still appears to be up. Single maintainer is a red flag for long-term reliability, and the project is not widely known/adopted.
client_requirements: Single CLI/binary install via `curl https://get.telebit.io/ | bash` (installs a Node.js-based client). No TUN/TAP interface; no root/admin required for basic `telebit http <port>` usage (uses application-layer HTTPS/TLS tunneling, not a VPN). Requires device 'claiming' via email confirmation, which adds friction for fully automated/headless provisioning.
server_requirements: Server source code is available in the same JS repo (it's a combined client+server Node.js codebase), so self-hosting is technically possible, though docs/support for running your own server independently of telebit.cloud are thin and mostly undocumented/community-figured-out. It is fundamentally a Node.js daemon; no separate first-class REST/control-plane API is documented for programmatic tunnel registration — provisioning is designed around the email-claim CLI flow, not an API you'd call from a backend.
has_programmable_api: false (or unclear) — JavaScript/Node.js codebase; no documented external HTTP API for registering tunnels programmatically. The Node.js server library could theoretically be embedded/imported into another Node app, but there's no supported SvelteKit-callable REST control-plane.
viability_notes: Client constraint is fine (simple CLI, no TUN/root), and it's genuinely open source with a permissive MIT license, but the ecosystem is essentially a single-maintainer side project with negligible adoption, poor documentation for self-hosting, and no clean programmatic API for our SvelteKit backend to hit. Not dead, but too obscure/fragile to build on with confidence.

name: tunnel.pyjam.as
license: Open source (permissive; per awesome-tunneling listing) — exact SPDX not independently confirmed beyond a LICENSE file present in repo
popularity: Very low visibility: hosted on GitLab (not GitHub), no star/fork counts surfaced in normal search; essentially a personal/small project by a single author (Asbjørn Kofoed-Nielsen). Not a widely adopted tool.
maturity: Repo exists with a CI pipeline (recent commit 'Remove javascript from index.html'), so it isn't completely abandoned, but it's a small, low-traffic project with no release/version cadence visible. Effectively a single-maintainer service.
client_requirements: FAILS the client constraint outright: per the awesome-tunneling list, tunnel.pyjam.as has 'No custom client; uses WireGuard directly instead.' That means the client must set up a WireGuard interface (a VPN kernel/userspace network interface), which is exactly the TUN/TAP-style requirement we must avoid, and typically needs elevated privileges to configure.
server_requirements: Server source available (Python, on GitLab). No separate documented REST/control-plane API for third-party backends to call — it's WireGuard-config driven.
has_programmable_api: false — it's a WireGuard config generator/service, not an HTTP API for tunnel registration from an external app.
viability_notes: Hard-fails our primary constraint because it relies on the client running WireGuard (a VPN network interface) rather than a simple binary/CLI, and it also lacks any programmable HTTP control-plane. Low adoption and single-maintainer status compound the risk. Not viable for our use case.

name: SSH-J.com
license: Not clearly published as a distinct client/server library license — this is essentially a public hosted SSH server configuration/service, not a packaged software project with its own release artifacts.
language: N/A — it is a public, anonymous SSH jump/port-forwarding server (based on dropbear SSH), not a distributable client or server codebase we would deploy ourselves.
popularity: No GitHub stars/forks (Bitbucket-hosted, single small repo). Known within the awesome-tunneling / self-hosting community as a free public utility, but not a software project with adoption metrics — it's a single public instance, also reachable over Tor onion service.
maturity: Appears to be a long-running personal hosted service by ValdikSS (also accessible via Tor onion), still live per its landing page (ssh-j.com), but has essentially no development activity to speak of — it's a static SSH server config, not actively 'released' software. Fundamentally a single operator's hosted service — classic bus-factor/abandonment risk (if the operator stops hosting it, the service disappears).
client_requirements: Explicitly 'No software, no registration' — just an ordinary SSH client (`ssh -R ...`), which every OS already ships. This is arguably the simplest possible client requirement: no custom binary, no TUN/TAP, no admin/root needed to run `ssh -R`. Excellent fit for the client-side constraint.
server_requirements: There is no server source code to self-host — SSH-J.com IS the server, run by a third party (ValdikSS) as a public shared multi-tenant service, limited to 50 exposed ports/username, intended only for SSH-to-SSH forwarding (they explicitly discourage exposing raw non-SSH public ports). We cannot host our own instance from published source, and there is no HTTP/REST control-plane at all — it's raw SSH port-forwarding semantics only.
server_language: N/A (dropbear SSH server, C, but not really an installable 'product' — it's a specific person's server configuration)
has_programmable_api: false — no API of any kind; it's raw `ssh -R`/`-J` semantics with no control-plane, and we don't control or host the server ourselves.
viability_notes: Client side is ideal (plain ssh, zero install), but this fails our other hard requirement: it's a third-party shared public service with no self-hostable server source and zero programmatic API — we cannot register/manage tunnels from our own backend, and we can't run 'our own' server binary since the software isn't really packaged for redistribution. Not usable for our architecture.

name: Greenhouse
popularity: Minimal: 0 stars, 0 forks, 2 watchers on its self-hosted Gitea instance (git.sequentialread.com). Niche project by a solo developer ('forest'/SequentialRead), not tracked on GitHub, no meaningful adoption signal found.
maturity: Effectively abandoned/stalled: last substantive activity was years ago (README last updated ~5 years ago per commit history, a security doc updated ~3 years ago), and per the awesome-tunneling list itself: 'The hosted service (greenhouse.server.garden) is currently unavailable and the project appears unmaintained (last activity 2023).' Explicit red flag of a dead hosted service and single-maintainer abandonment.
client_requirements: Designed to be a lightweight port-forwarding client with automatic HTTPS ('least-authority' design so the service never holds your TLS private keys), which in principle sounds admin-free, but with the project dead and hosted service down, this is moot — there is no functioning client/server pairing to evaluate in practice today.
server_requirements: Full server source is available (Go, self-hostable), including an admin panel with token-based API keys (public_api.go, threshold_provisioning_service.go) suggesting some HTTP-based control API existed for the hosted alpha/beta service, but there's no current documentation, it's unmaintained, and the hosted reference instance is down — reviving/self-hosting it would require significant unsupported reverse-engineering effort.
has_programmable_api: Possibly true historically (Go) — code includes a 'public_api.go' and multiple API tokens per the commit history — but undocumented, unmaintained, and unverifiable as currently working.
viability_notes: Interesting design goals (least-authority, no custom client TLS key handoff) but the project and its hosted service are dead, it's a single-maintainer effort with zero community adoption, and any API surface is undocumented and unmaintained. Not a safe foundation to build production tunneling on.

name: frp
popularity: Extremely popular: 109.5k GitHub stars, 15.2k forks, 1.6k watchers, 1,524+ commits. One of the most widely used open-source reverse-proxy/tunnel tools; has an active related-projects ecosystem (gofrp/plugin, gofrp/tiny-frpc), CI badges, GitHub Sponsors, and corporate sponsors (JetBrains, RapidProxy, Olares). Very strong, long-standing adoption signal.
maturity: Actively maintained: dev branch under continuous development, recent feature-gate/experimental-feature system documented (ALPHA/BETA/GA lifecycle), ongoing releases via GitHub Releases and CircleCI. No abandonment red flags — large contributor base, not single-maintainer dependent for day-to-day operation despite fatedier being lead.
client_requirements: Single static Go binary (frpc) — no TUN/TAP, no admin/root required for standard TCP/HTTP/HTTPS proxying (root only needed if binding to privileged ports <1024, same as any normal server software). Config-file driven (TOML) but can also be driven via CLI flags/env vars. There's also a 'tiny-frpc' variant (~3.5MB) for constrained devices. Overall this is an excellent, simple client story.
server_requirements: Full server (frps) source code available in the same repo (Go). frps does expose an HTTP-based Admin API / Dashboard (documented in the frp docs, e.g. `/api/*` endpoints for reload, proxy status, server info) that can be queried, though it's primarily geared toward admin/monitoring and reload-of-config rather than a full first-class 'create tunnel' REST resource-oriented API for provisioning arbitrary tunnels at runtime without config. Frp's typical model is: client authenticates with a token and requests proxies itself (proxies are largely declared in the frpc config, though frpc also has features for env-var and dynamic config, and there's an admin API on the client side too). It's more 'config/token-driven binary with a monitoring/admin HTTP API' than a full programmatic-tunnel-creation REST API, but it is scriptable and self-hostable, and the wire protocol/API is documented enough that a backend could plausibly automate it (e.g., by templating frpc config and restarting/reloading, or via its client admin API).
has_programmable_api: Partially true — Go; frps/frpc expose an HTTP Admin API (dashboard, reload, proxy/traffic stats) documented in frp's docs, and frpc supports config reload without restart. It is not a purpose-built 'POST /tunnels' REST API for on-demand tunnel registration, but the admin API + reload mechanism + token auth model gives a workable path to drive it programmatically from a backend.
viability_notes: Best-in-class maturity, adoption, and client simplicity (single static Go binary, no TUN/root) make frp a very strong candidate; the main gap versus a 'true' JS/TS control-plane API is that tunnel provisioning is more config/reload-oriented than resource-style REST, requiring us to write glue code (config templating + reload, or driving the admin API) rather than calling a clean 'create tunnel' endpoint. Still a top pick given its maturity and self-hostability.

name: ngrok 1.0
popularity: 24.4k GitHub stars, 4.3k forks — historically very popular (2013-2016 era, the tool that essentially popularized this whole category), but that popularity is legacy/historical rather than current.
maturity: Explicitly dead as an open-source project: GitHub shows 'This repository was archived by the owner on Jun 3, 2024. It is now read-only,' and the README states plainly: 'This is the GitHub repository for the old v1 version of ngrok which was actively developed from 2013-2016... This repository is archived: ngrok v1 is no longer developed, supported or maintained.' The commercial ngrok 2.0+ service continues, but that is closed-source with its own API/SDKs (ngrok-go, ngrok-javascript, ngrok-python, etc.) — a different product entirely from this archived open-source repo.
client_requirements: N/A for our purposes — codebase is unmaintained/archived and the original hosted ngrokd service this client talked to is long gone; self-hosting v1 today would require reviving 8+ year old Go code with no support.
server_requirements: Source (ngrokd) is technically available in the archived repo (Go), so in theory it could be self-hosted/forked, but there is zero ongoing maintenance, no security patching, and no programmable control-plane API documented for v1.
has_programmable_api: false for this v1 codebase — no documented control-plane API; the JS/Python/Go/Rust/Java 'agent SDKs' mentioned on the archived README belong to the separate, closed-source ngrok 2.0+ commercial product, not this repo.
viability_notes: Explicitly archived/abandoned by its own maintainer in favor of a closed-source commercial successor — a clear-cut dead project despite its large historical star count. Not viable to build on; the only 'API' ecosystem (ngrok agent SDKs) belongs to the commercial closed-source ngrok, which is out of scope since we need open source.

name: Pangolin
license: Dual-licensed: AGPL-3.0 (open source) and Fossorial Commercial License (for commercial use cases)
language: TypeScript / Next.js (server + dashboard); companion client 'newt' is Go
popularity: 22.8k GitHub stars, 786 forks, 71 watchers, 8,469+ commits — very actively developed and increasingly popular self-hosted SASE/zero-trust platform. Its client connector 'newt' has its own repo with 909 stars / 87 forks. Explicitly recommended in the awesome-tunneling README as one of two 'production ready' self-hosted options (alongside frp).
maturity: Very actively maintained: huge, continuously growing commit history (8,469 commits), current feature work includes an 'AI Gateway,' recent architecture docs, and an official hosted Pangolin Cloud offering alongside self-hosting — strong signal of ongoing investment, not a single-maintainer side project (fosrl org, commercial backing).
client_requirements: The client connector, 'newt,' is a single static Go binary (get-newt.sh install script; also packaged for Windows via Inno Setup, Nix flake, Docker). Critically, newt implements WireGuard fully in userspace via netstack (gVisor's userspace TCP/IP stack) rather than creating a kernel TUN/TAP device — per its own README: 'it will use the information encoded (endpoint, public key) to bring up a WireGuard tunnel using netstack... fully in user space.' This means no OS-level TUN/TAP interface and no admin/root privileges are required to run it — it registers with the Pangolin server over HTTP+WebSocket using an ID/secret, a good fit for our constraint.
server_requirements: Full server source available (TypeScript/Next.js control plane + Go 'Gerbil' WireGuard exit-node component), self-hostable via Docker Compose. Newt registers with Pangolin via plain HTTP requests to get a session token, then holds a WebSocket for control messages — i.e., there IS a documented HTTP+WebSocket control-plane protocol between client and server, though the full public developer-facing REST API surface for third-party backends (e.g., 'create site/resource via our own code') would need confirming against docs.pangolin.net, but the architecture (identity, sites, resources, clients all as first-class managed objects in a Next.js/TypeScript control plane) strongly suggests a workable admin API exists for programmatic registration.
server_language: TypeScript (Next.js control plane), Go (Gerbil exit-node / WireGuard component)
has_programmable_api: Likely true — TypeScript; Pangolin's control plane is a TypeScript/Next.js app with organized resources (sites, resources, clients, identity/access) and a documented registration handshake (HTTP session token + WebSocket control channel) used by the newt client itself, implying an internal REST/WS API that a SvelteKit backend could potentially call or emulate, though full public API docs would need direct verification for a supported 'register tunnel' surface.
viability_notes: Best overall fit: hosted server binary/Docker deployment is expected and well-documented, the client (newt) is a single Go binary using userspace WireGuard (no TUN/TAP, no root) satisfying our hardest constraint, and the control plane is TypeScript with an HTTP+WebSocket registration protocol that aligns closely with 'hittable control-plane from our SvelteKit backend.' Very active development and strong adoption reduce abandonment risk versus the other candidates. Top pick.

name: chisel
popularity: 16.5k GitHub stars, 1.6k forks, 207 watchers, 261 commits. Well-established, widely used utility (also packaged for Fedora/EPEL, Docker Hub + GHCR images), commonly cited as an ngrok/SSH-tunnel alternative.
maturity: Actively maintained: recent changelog entries describe substantive v1.12 changes (SOCKS5 authfile enforcement, SHA256 fingerprint requirements, graceful shutdown, UDP connection caps, Go 1.27.0 builds, updated x/crypto/ssh to address a CVE) — clear evidence of an actively developed, security-conscious release cadence, not a stalled project. Single primary maintainer (Jaime Pillora) but healthy release/issue activity.
client_requirements: Single static Go binary combining both client and server (`chisel client`, `chisel server`); no TUN/TAP interface, no admin/root required for typical use (transports TCP/UDP over HTTP secured via SSH protocol under the hood, entirely in userspace). Trivial install via `curl .../chisel! | bash`, Docker, `go install`, or OS packages. Excellent fit for the client constraint — arguably as simple as it gets.
server_requirements: Full source available (single Go repo, MIT licensed); the 'chisel server' binary is what we'd host. However, it is fundamentally a CLI/flag-driven binary (e.g., `chisel server --port $PORT --backend ...`) with no HTTP REST control-plane / admin API of its own for creating or managing tunnels at runtime — tunnels are established by clients connecting and requesting specific remote forwards via the CLI/protocol, not via a management API we'd call from a backend. There's no separate provisioning API to hit; any orchestration (e.g., generating per-user auth tokens via `--authfile`, spawning/killing server processes) would have to be built by us around the binary.
has_programmable_api: false as a control-plane — Go source is embeddable as a library (chisel is importable as a Go package, e.g., github.com/jpillora/chisel/server), which is useful if our backend were Go, but there's no JS/TS/HTTP-native control-plane API; from a SvelteKit backend we would only be able to shell out to / manage the binary and its authfile/config, not call a REST API to register tunnels.
viability_notes: Chisel is mature, popular, and has by far the simplest possible client (single static binary, zero TUN/root), making it a very strong operational fit; the downside relative to Pangolin is the total lack of any HTTP/TS control-plane — we'd have to build our own glue (authfile management, process control) around a config/CLI-driven binary rather than calling an API. Solid fallback if Pangolin's control plane doesn't pan out.

name: rathole
popularity: 14.2k stars, 827 forks, 73 watchers; widely used as an frp/ngrok alternative, Docker Hub image (rapiz1/rathole) with active pulls, active Gitter chat community
maturity: Actively maintained (234 commits, ongoing releases with semver tags and CI badge); no obvious red flags, but the project's own 'Planning' section lists 'HTTP APIs for configuration' as still work-in-progress (not yet shipped), so dynamic/API-driven tunnel registration is not fully available today (hot-reload via config file is supported instead).
client_requirements: Single static Rust binary (~500KiB minimal build) for both client and server, no TAP/TUN interface, no admin/root required, no complex install — just run the binary with a TOML config. Meets constraints well.
server_requirements: Full server source code available (same repo, Rust). Server is config-file (TOML) driven with hot-reload of the config file; a built-in HTTP control-plane API is explicitly listed as 'WIP' / planned but not confirmed shipped, so today it is essentially a config-driven binary, not a REST API you can hit to register tunnels programmatically.
has_programmable_api: false — an HTTP API for configuration is only planned/WIP per the README, not a confirmed shipped feature; current control is via TOML config file hot-reload only.
viability_notes: Excellent fit on the client side (tiny static binary, no admin, no TUN) and server source is open and lightweight, but lacks a confirmed working HTTP control-plane API today, meaning our SvelteKit backend would have to manage tunnels by writing/hot-reloading TOML config files rather than calling a REST API. Good fallback option if we're willing to shell out to config-file management.

name: sshuttle
popularity: 13.6k stars, 794 forks, 134 watchers; long-standing popular 'poor man's VPN' tool, widely referenced in sysadmin/security tooling lists
maturity: Actively maintained (1,363 commits, ongoing releases, uses modern tooling like uv/pyproject.toml); mature and stable project with no major red flags for its intended use case.
client_requirements: FAILS constraint. Despite README claims of 'doesn't require admin', sshuttle works as a transparent proxy/VPN-like tool: it uses iptables/pf firewall rules and typically must run the local sshuttle process as root (or with sudo) on the client to set up NAT/firewall redirection to route all matching traffic through the SSH tunnel; on the client it needs elevated privileges to manipulate the routing/firewall tables, which is effectively equivalent to VPN-style setup even though it avoids a literal TUN/TAP kernel driver in most modes. This is a fundamentally different (transparent-proxy) usage model than a simple reverse tunnel client, and not what we need.
server_requirements: Server-side just needs plain SSH access (uses the remote user's Python via SSH, no separate daemon/API); no server source needed beyond stock sshd — but this is irrelevant given the client fails our hard constraint.
server_language: Python (assembled/pushed over SSH at connect time)
has_programmable_api: false — no HTTP API; it's purely a CLI wrapping SSH + local firewall manipulation.
viability_notes: sshuttle is architecturally a whole-network transparent VPN-like proxy, not a single-service reverse tunnel; its client requires root/admin to configure firewall/NAT rules, directly violating our no-admin constraint. Also has no programmable server API — it's just SSH. Not suitable for our use case.

name: bore
popularity: 11.5k stars, 528 forks, 62 watchers; packaged on Homebrew, AUR, Gentoo overlay, crates.io (bore-cli), public hosted instance at bore.pub
maturity: Actively maintained relative to its scope (68 commits — intentionally minimal, ~400 lines of code); has CI, versioned Docker images and crates.io releases. No red flags, but it is a deliberately minimal project (no plans for a control-plane API, by design philosophy of doing 'one thing').
client_requirements: Single static Rust binary (`bore local <port> --to <server>`), installable via Homebrew/AUR/Cargo/prebuilt release binaries or Docker. No TAP/TUN, no admin/root needed. Excellent fit.
server_requirements: Full server source available (same repo). Server is a single binary (`bore server`) configured entirely via CLI flags/env vars (min/max port range, bind address, optional shared secret) — no config file and no HTTP control-plane/REST API at all; tunnels are created dynamically by the client itself via the control-port protocol (not by pushing registrations from an external system).
has_programmable_api: false — no HTTP/REST API; only a lightweight custom TCP control protocol between client and server, driven from the client side, not something a SvelteKit backend can call directly to register tunnels for other machines.
viability_notes: Ideal on the client side (trivial static binary, no admin, no TUN) and the server is fully open-source and simple to self-host, but there is no HTTP control-plane/API to register or manage tunnels from our own backend — tunnel creation is driven only by the client's own connection to the server. Good if our backend can just tell the client to run 'bore local', less good if we need central orchestration.

name: gost
popularity: 7.5k stars, 828 forks, 52 watchers; large multi-protocol proxy/tunnel toolkit with companion GUI (gostctl) and WebUI (gost-ui) projects, active Telegram/Google Group community
maturity: Actively maintained (558 commits, continuous releases, install script, Docker images, dedicated docs site gost.run); broad protocol support (websocket, grpc, quic, kcp, etc.) and a documented Web API — no major red flags.
client_requirements: Single Go binary, installable via releases page, install script, or Docker; used as a reverse-proxy/tunnel client with no admin/root required. Note: gost ALSO supports optional TUN/TAP device modes for VPN-like use cases, but that is an optional feature — for a plain reverse-proxy/tunnel client (websocket/TCP forwarding) it runs as a normal unprivileged process. Meets constraints as long as TUN/TAP mode is avoided.
server_requirements: Full server source available (same repo, Go). Server exposes a genuine RESTful Web API (`-api` flag or `api:` config block) with HTTP Basic Auth, configurable path prefix, access logging, and a built-in Swagger/OpenAPI spec (testable at api.gost.run/swagger-ui) for dynamically creating/listing/removing services, listeners, and chains at runtime — this is a real hittable control-plane, not just a config file.
has_programmable_api: true — Go server with a documented RESTful HTTP API (Basic Auth, Swagger/OpenAPI spec) for dynamic runtime configuration of services/tunnels; can be called from any backend including a SvelteKit/Node app via plain HTTP requests.
viability_notes: Strong candidate: single unprivileged Go binary client, open server source, and a real documented REST API with Swagger docs for dynamically registering tunnels/services — exactly the kind of control-plane we want to hit from SvelteKit. Slight complexity cost is gost's very large feature surface (many protocols/concepts to learn) versus more minimal tools.

name: tunnelto
popularity: 7.1k stars, 546 forks, 49 watchers; published on crates.io as 'wormhole-tunnel'/'tunnelto', Homebrew tap, Docker image, hosted commercial service at tunnelto.dev
maturity: Moderate activity (119 commits); README shows Cargo.toml pinned near v0.1.14 and a note that self-hosted deployments do not support multi-instance/centralized coordination (the real distributed version is proprietary, running on fly.io). This is a meaningful limitation/red flag for production self-hosting at scale, though basic single-instance self-hosting works.

viability_notes: Only viable if we invert Wiretap's own terminology: put the unprivileged, TUN-free 'wiretap serve' binary on the end-user's local machine, and accept that our hosted infrastructure runs the actual privileged WireGuard peer.
